ShareSecret vs DeleteSecret across replicas: a share INSERT racing the #370 cascade committed live on the deleted secret and reactivated on RestoreSecret. CreateShareRecord now writes then re-reads the secret FOR SHARE in one transaction and rolls back if it is gone (INV-STORE-21); covers both B-before-insert and B-after-insert interleavings
ShareSecretWithGroup vs DeleteSecret across replicas: same CreateShareRecord window as #2646 for a group share; closed by the same write-then-FOR-SHARE parent re-check (INV-STORE-21)

GrantSecretACL vs DeleteSecret across replicas: an ACL upsert racing the CWE-284 cascade committed on the deleted secret and reactivated on RestoreSecret. CreateOrUpdateSecretACL now upserts then re-reads the secret node FOR SHARE in one transaction and rolls back if it is gone (INV-STORE-21); single-process half: TestLocalACL_RefusesSoftDeletedSecret

CreateDynamicSecretConfig vs DeleteProject across replicas: the post-insert full-row Save wrote disabled=false back over the #369 cascade disable, leaving an enabled config in a deleted project that mints again on restore. The DSN write is now a targeted UPDATE (SetDynamicSecretConfigAdminDSN), and the insert re-reads the project FOR SHARE in its transaction (INV-STORE-21); sibling: _DeleteProjectAfterInsert_

IssueLease vs DeleteProject across replicas: a lease inserted while the #369 cascade disabled its config was never listed by the post-commit revocation, leaving a live database credential under a deleted project until TTL. CreateDynamicSecretLease now inserts an active lease then re-reads the config (enabled) FOR SHARE in one transaction and rolls back if disabled; IssueLease revokes the minted credential (INV-STORE-21); single-process half: TestCreateDynamicSecretLease_ActiveRefusedOnDisabledConfig

RestoreEnvironment vs DeleteProject across replicas: the project-liveness check and the un-delete were separate statements and the cascade swept environments before touching the project row, leaving a live environment under a deleted project. RestoreEnvironment now un-deletes then re-reads the project FOR SHARE in one transaction; deleteProjectCascade row-locks the project before any child sweep (INV-STORE-21). Siblings: _vs_DeleteProject_, _DeleteProjectAfterUpdate_

SetDynamicSecretConfigEnabled had no parent-liveness check, so a dynamic-secret config could be re-enabled while its project was soft-deleted — invisible in every project-scoped view, and live again the moment someone restored the project, with no re-authorization at that point (#369/#370 restore-reactivation class). Enabling now requires a live project via the soft-delete-scoped GetProject; disabling stays ungated (the safe direction). Found by GUARD-5 ordering sweep under a SERIAL ordering, so not a race: distinct from #2651, whose racing path #2675 fixes separately.

ActivateMFA/DisableMFA: a panic in resolveKeepSession GetSession (after the change committed) reported the committed MFA change as failed and skipped the post-change session purge, leaving other sessions live. The panic now takes the existing fail-closed full-purge fallback (INV-CORE-34 class)

A login (and every other session-issuing op: MFA verify, WebAuthn finish, SAML ACS, OIDC callback, impersonation start, refresh) that reported failure left a live Session the client never received: a panic in the post-mint identity read or step-up grant write, or CreateSession/RotateSession effect-then-error. Identity is now resolved before the mint, post-mint best-effort writes are panic-safe, and a session write that errored is read back by token (delivered if it landed; deleted and audited on panic). Oracle (f) in checkOraclesReporting plus TestUndeliveredSessionSweep guard the class

finalizeAccessRequestApproval granted the role, recorded the approval, and updated the request state as three SEPARATE writes with a compensating revertGrant covering a failure in the last two. The compensation got the end STATE right, but a reported failure still left revertGrant's own "approval_race_reverted" AuditEvent row behind -- the operation's only observable effect for a request the caller was told had failed -- which FuzzStorageFaultOperations' oracle (a) flagged (REST PUT /api/v1/projects/{id}/access-requests/{requestId}, CreateAccessRequestApproval#1/error). It also left a real TOCTOU window in which the role was genuinely granted before being revoked. Fixed in #2415: grant + approval record + request-state update run inside ONE storage.WithTransaction, so a reported failure means precisely "nothing happened". Proving test asserts the EFFECT (zero new audit rows after a reported failure), not a return value; verified non-vacuous by replacing internal/core/invitations.go with its 7d9d31d6^ content, against which it goes red ("expected: 0, actual: 3"). NOT guarded by a committed fuzz seed, deliberately: replaying the issue's own input against that same pre-fix file PASSES, because onlyOutcomeLogTables accepts an AuditEvent-only diff by design and short-circuits before the oracle reports -- a seed named for #2407 would certify the unfixed code as correct. See the removed knownOpenTolerances entry's replacement comment in server/faultops/fuzz_storage_fault_operations_test.go for the full measurement.

Found live by FuzzAuthCacheDifferential (FUZZ-GAPS G5) within seconds of its first fuzzing run, not a hand-written seed. setAccountState (internal/core/account_state.go), the shared implementation behind SuspendUser/ReactivateUser/RequirePasswordReset/etc, collected every one of the target user's session AND personal-access-token hashes and evicted them from the HTTP auth cache via customMiddleware.InvalidateTokenCacheByHash for EVERY account-state transition, including a transition INTO plain active (ReactivateUser) -- but InvalidateTokenCacheByHash does not do a plain delete; per its own doc comment it writes a short-lived NEGATIVE tombstone so an in-flight positive validation racing a real revoke can't resurrect a stale entry. Writing that tombstone unconditionally meant a personal access token created WHILE an account is suspended, then swept by that SAME account's later reactivation, was spuriously rejected (401) for up to invalidTokenTTL even though it had never been cached before and the account was already active again -- oracle: the auth decision computed with the cache disagreed with the decision computed with the cache bypassed, for a token neither revoked nor expired. Fixed by scoping the proactive eviction sweep to only run when the TARGET state is more restrictive than plain active (AccountLoginBlocked || AccountRestricted) -- moving toward active never needed a proactive evict for correctness: an over-restrictive stale cache entry is safe (fail-closed), and any EXISTING positive entry already gets AccountState/Restricted refreshed on every hit by serveAuthCacheHit's own re-check, independent of this sweep. Red-before/green-after proving test creates a PAT while suspended, reactivates, and asserts the PAT authenticates on its very first use.

validateAdminDSNHost (internal/core/dynamic_secrets.go) silently skipped SSRF validation for an ENTIRE PostgreSQL multi-host admin_dsn the moment any one host in the comma-separated list was a bracket-quoted IPv6 literal (RFC 3986 requires the brackets, and PostgreSQL's own multi-host URI syntax permits mixing bracketed-IPv6 and plain-IPv4 hosts in one list, e.g. postgres://user@8.8.8.8:5432,[64:ff9b::169.254.169.254]:5432/db). Go's net/url.Parse rejects that shape outright (treats everything after the closing bracket as a single port component and errors the moment it isn't pure digits: invalid port ":5432,[...]" after host) even though pgx.ParseConfig -- the actual driver dialPostgres (internal/dynamic/postgres.go) uses -- parses and connects to it without complaint (confirmed directly against both). parseDSNHostsFromURL's only path returned (nil, false) on that url.Parse error, parseDSNHosts then found no other format match, and validateAdminDSNHost's "unrecognised format, can't extract host" branch treated the WHOLE DSN as unvalidatable -- a NAT64/6to4/Teredo/native-IPv6-encoded private or cloud-IMDS host anywhere in such a list sailed through registration completely unchecked while pgx would actually dial it. Found live by FuzzSSRFGuardDifferential, a new differential fuzzer driving one address through every independent SSRF guard in the codebase (netutil.IsPrivateOrLinkLocal/IsLinkLocal, the SIEM forwarder's and notification-channel webhook guard's own disallow policies, the connect/OIDC-JWKS Dialer{Disallow: IsLinkLocal} wiring, and validateAdminDSNHost) for encoding-parity and multi-host-DSN coverage neither FuzzIPv4EmbeddingSSRFParity nor FuzzAdminDSNHostSSRFGuard's own documented follow-up gap covered. Fixed by manualAuthorityHosts, a url.Parse-independent fallback that extracts the host-list authority segment by direct string scanning (bypassing url.Parse's authority grammar entirely) whenever url.Parse itself rejects the DSN; splitDSNHostList was also hardened to strip stray brackets from a port-less bracketed IPv6 entry. Red-before/green-after: reverting manualAuthorityHosts to return nil, false reproduces the bypass on 6 of 10 fuzz seeds (MULTI-HOST SSRF BYPASS (validateAdminDSNHost, URL multi-host): wantPrivate=true ... err=<nil>); restoring it returns all seeds plus the retained corpus entry to PASS. See the PR body for full red-proof output.

admin restore was index-blind to WHEN a backup was taken relative to subsequent legitimate changes: restoring an archive older than what this host had already certified silently resurrected any access revoked since (a suspended account, a deleted machine credential, a rotated role grant) -- the restored database simply does not know the revocation happened, and verify-audit correctly reports the restored (shorter, self-consistent) chain as VALID either way, since a bare hash-chain re-walk cannot distinguish "shorter but genuinely older" from "truncated." design-b3-backup-v2.md section 6.3 implements the fix: admin backup records the source install's own signed audit high-water mark (system_metadata audit_checkpoint_highwater) in MANIFEST.json; every server mirrors that same mark to a host-local witness file (.audit-highwater-witness, sibling to the database, internal/core advanceAuditHighWater) as it advances; admin restore compares the archive value against the witness value BEFORE writing anything to disk and refuses if the archive is behind, requiring an explicit --allow-rollback (which itself writes an audit event recording the override) to proceed. Red-before/green-after: TestAdminRestore_RefusesRollback_WithoutOverride reproduces the exact repro (an older backup restoring silently, verify-audit reporting VALID) when the check is disabled, and refuses it with the fix in place.

a campaign revoke whose grant removal failed left the item stamped revoked while the grant was still live (false ISO 27001 A.5.18 / SOC 2 CC6.2-6.3 evidence) and un-retryable; claim + removal + audit now run in one transaction so a failed apply rolls the claim back

the fault-free instance of the same defect and the anti-drift guard: a last-project-admin guard REFUSAL (an ordinary expected outcome, no fault injection) also used to stamp the item revoked; it now leaves it pending, and the assertion fails if the access-review path ever stops reusing the public removal path lock+guard wrapper

the same rollback against real Postgres, which aborts a transaction on a failing statement rather than SQLites more forgiving semantics - a rollback path that works on SQLite is not evidence it works here

the lock-ordering review #2676 asked for: two reviewers on independent connections revoking different items that share one projectAdminGuardLockKey, each holding its own transaction, must both complete - pins named-lock-outside/transaction-inside and the two-pooled-connection budget (pgOpen MaxOpenConns(2)) a third connection inside the transaction would break

DeleteAuditLogsBefore deleted by event_time < cutoff; when id order and event_time order disagree (concurrent writers, HA clock skew) it removed a mid-chain row and VerifyAuditChain reported tampering. Now deletes only the contiguous id prefix of old rows (subset of the old delete) under the KEYAUDIT lock; INV-STORE-22. AWSIAMExecutor.GenerateUpstream accepted a rotation whose CreateAccessKey response carried non-nil pointers to "" for AccessKeyId/SecretAccessKey -- the guard checked only created.AccessKey.AccessKeyId/SecretAccessKey == nil, never the pointed-to string's content; fixed by also requiring aws.ToString(...) != "" on both fields; fuzz-confirmed (#2209)

client.Encrypt (internal/crypto/awskms/awskms.go) returned a KMS Encrypt response's CiphertextBlob completely unchecked; a 2xx response with a missing/empty/null CiphertextBlob was treated as a successful wrap. kms_provider.go's generateAndWrap then persisted this empty blob verbatim to the wrapped-KEK file via securefiles.SecureWriteFileSync (which also has no length check) -- first-run startup appeared to succeed, but the persisted file was unusable on the next restart. Found by a private pre-disclosure fuzzing pass on aws-sdk-go-v2's KMS client (mirror harness, since internal/ packages are cross-module unimportable); structurally identical to the already-fixed awssm.go SecretString=="" gap (docs/findings/2026-09-20-FINDING-awssm-empty-secret-response.md). Fixed by rejecting a zero-length CiphertextBlob as an error rather than returning it; red-before/green-after proving test confirmed by reverting the fix and re-running.

AWSSecretsManagerConnector.GetSecret returned success with "" when SecretString was present but empty ({"SecretString":""}) -- out.SecretString != nil is true for a pointer to an empty string, not just to real content; fixed by also requiring *out.SecretString != ""; found by FuzzAWSSMConnectorResponse (crasher 09de4b520b95a429, committed as a seed), fixed same PR; dedicated point test used as the proving test (not the fuzzer) so this claim has its own unambiguous test name, matching the connect-response-size-cap-aws-001/-azure-001 convention; see docs/findings/2026-09-20-FINDING-awssm-empty-secret-response.md

AWSSTSEngine.Issue accepted a successful AssumeRole whose Credentials.AccessKeyId/SecretAccessKey/SessionToken were non-nil pointers to "" -- out.Credentials == nil is true only when the struct itself is absent, not when its string fields are empty; fixed by also requiring aws.ToString(...) != "" on all three fields; fuzz-confirmed (#2210)

AzureKeyVaultConnector.GetSecret had the identical defect as its AWS sibling (out.Value == nil, no empty-string guard) -- a response like {"value":""} returned success with an empty value; fixed by also requiring *out.Value != ""; the fuzzer's own oracle had the same pointer-only blind spot as the connector code, so it was strengthened too (now requires *ref.Value != ""), with a new {"value":""} seed added to lock in coverage; dedicated point test used as the proving test because FuzzAzureKVConnectorResponse is already the proving test for the unrelated connect-redirect-refusal-001 claim, and check-closures.sh's claim-name lookup does not disambiguate two claims sharing one (package, test) pair; see docs/findings/2026-09-20-FINDING-awssm-empty-secret-response.md

ActivateBreakGlass inserted the activation record (state=active) and then granted the emergency role as two separate storage operations with no shared transaction and no lock, while RevokeBreakGlassActivationAtomic did its own pair under projectAdminGuardLockKey and deliberately TOLERATES ErrRoleNotAssigned ("already gone -- proceed to reconcile the record"). A revoke landing between the activation's two writes therefore removed nothing, transitioned the record to revoked, audited success, and the activation then granted the emergency role anyway. End state: a self-granted, SoD-bypassing role live for its full TTL while the record every reviewer and the UI reads says revoked -- and because the admin's revoke reported success nobody revisits it; ReconcileExpired only touches active rows so it never cleans it up; and the freed partial-unique-index slot lets the user activate a second time. Fixed by running the insert and the grant inside ONE acquisition of the SAME key the revoke takes, with the pair extracted into activateBreakGlassLocked so the two writes cannot be separated without the guard noticing; the audit and admin notification stay outside the lock, after the grant commits. NOT fixed with lockLiveParent, which is how every other fix in this class is built and which #2722's own suggested direction proposed: lockLiveParent requires the delete side to row-lock the PARENT before touching the children, and this revoke does the opposite (tx.RemoveRole runs BEFORE tx.RevokeBreakGlassActivation), so a FOR SHARE on the activation row would be read after the revoke had already looked for and not found the grant, and the race would survive the fix. Lock-order safety: one acquisition at family rank 3 with nothing nested inside, no inversion against storage.NamedLockOrder. This row is the structural default-ci guard, which also pins that the REVOKE still takes the same key -- dropping it there would silently reopen the race with nothing else going red. Red-proven by calling activateBreakGlassLocked without the lock: this guard fails, and so do both pg-gated tests (see break-glass-grant-survives-revoke-002)

The behavioural half of break-glass-grant-survives-revoke-001, plus TestCTAReview_BreakGlassActivate_WaitsForTheRevokeLock_Postgres in the same file. The ctaReview beforeA hook every other fix in this class uses CANNOT be used here, and the reason is structural: beforeA runs replica B synchronously inside replica A's own callback on A's goroutine, so with A holding the named lock B would block inside A's call stack and the test would HANG rather than fail. So the serialization is proved two other ways. The lock-wait test holds projectAdminGuardLockKey on replica B -- the exact key the revoke takes -- and asserts A's activation does not complete until it is released, which is mutual exclusion with the revoke path without needing the revoke in flight. This row's named test races activate against revoke concurrently over 12 iterations and asserts the end-state invariant: if the revoke reported success, no live emergency grant may remain. It is probabilistic by construction and says so; it also carries a FLOOR requiring at least half the iterations to have produced a successfully-revoked activation, because without it the test is vacuous whenever B never manages a revoke -- which is not hypothetical: an earlier version passed exactly that way, since the activating user was not a project member so no activation existed to revoke, and only the lock-wait test caught it. Red-proven: with the lock removed, the concurrent test fails 3 of 3 runs with the exact reported end state (record revoked, revoke reported success, emergency role still granted) and the lock-wait test fails immediately with err=nil. Also fixed in the course of that proof: the lock-wait test released its advisory lock only on the happy path, so its own t.Fatalf left a goroutine holding it -- and a Postgres advisory lock is scoped to the DATABASE, not to the test's isolated schema, so it hung the parallel test for a full 600s timeout. The release is now a t.Cleanup; a test that hangs the suite on failure instead of failing is worse than no test

Found live by this same fix's own 10-minute fuzz-validation burst, same createuser-best-effort-panic-002/-003 shape: RevokeBreakGlassActivationAtomic's post-commit evictUserSessionCache call (internal/core/account.go) had no panic protection -- a panic there, after the role removal + activation-revoke had already committed, skipped the LogBreakGlassRevoked audit call that follows it and surfaced as a request failure despite the state having already fully changed, oracle (a): Differing tables [UserRole AuditEvent BreakGlassActivation]. Fixed at evictUserSessionCache's own single choke point (defer/recover + SECURITY log line, matching emitAudit's existing pattern) -- closes it for its other two call sites in rbac_management.go too, not just the one the fuzzer reached it through. Proving test is the fuzz harness itself -- corpus entry c3012b444731c557 is the permanent regression. See docs/findings/2026-09-23-FINDING-breakglass-revoke-half-commit.md. Regression-corpus fidelity note (2026-09-27): ADR-108 Phase 6 step 14c's opCatalog shrink silently retargeted this corpus file's decoded operation from "REST POST /api/v1/groups/{id}/members" to an unrelated op -- repaired by re-encoding the file's byte[0] to the same op's new index, verified to decode back to the original op/method/NthCall/kind tuple; guarded going forward by TestOpcatalogCorpusFilesTargetPinnedOps (server/faultops/opcatalog_corpus_pin_test.go).

Both break-glass revoke entry points (core.RevokeBreakGlass, backing the REST/gRPC human routes, and the /system RevokeBreakGlassActivationProxy) ran role removal and the activation-state update as two independent top-level storage calls, not one transaction -- an effect-then-error fault on RemoveRole (the DELETE lands, the call still reports failure) left the role gone but the activation still "active" and no break_glass.revoked audit event, oracle (d): Differing tables vs before [UserRole], vs reference [BreakGlassActivation AuditEvent]. Fixed by a new shared internal/core.RevokeBreakGlassActivationAtomic wrapping both storage calls in one storage.WithTransaction, called by both entry points; audit/cache-eviction moved to strictly after commit (CreateRole/UpdateRole's #1969/#1996 convention). No SAVEPOINT needed (verified against real Postgres, not just asserted): RemoveRole's tolerated "already gone" case is a zero-rows DELETE, not a genuine aborting SQL statement. Proving test is the fuzz harness itself -- corpus entry 7c0a2492ee5d1dfa is the permanent regression (red-before/green-after confirmed by reverting the fix in the dev worktree and replaying). See docs/findings/2026-09-23-FINDING-breakglass-revoke-half-commit.md. Regression-corpus fidelity note (2026-09-27): ADR-108 Phase 6 step 14c's opCatalog shrink silently retargeted this corpus file's decoded operation from "REST POST /api/v1/roles/" to an unrelated op -- repaired by re-encoding the file's byte[0] to the same op's new index, verified to decode back to the original op/method/NthCall/kind tuple; guarded going forward by TestOpcatalogCorpusFilesTargetPinnedOps (server/faultops/opcatalog_corpus_pin_test.go).

ClassifyMachineToken read a machine credential unlocked and persisted it through UpdateMachineIdentityCredential, a bare GORM Save of the WHOLE row -- so a RevokeMachineToken that committed on another replica between the read and the write was silently reverted (revoked=false written back), and the revoked, possibly leaked token authenticated again with nothing in the audit trail showing the un-revoke. Reachable over gRPC/HTTP with roles.assign on the project. Fixed by replacing the full-row primitive OUTRIGHT with SetMachineIdentityCredentialClassification, a conditional column-scoped UPDATE of classification alone gated on the value the caller read; machine_identity_credentials now has no full-row writer at all (revoked moves only via RevokeMachineIdentityCredential's UpdateColumn, last_used_at only via TouchMachineIdentityCredential). Red on real Postgres before the fix: the revoked token re-authenticated (ValidateMachineToken returned no error). Found by C-GUARD-3 guard 1

structural half of classify-machine-token-un-revoke-001 (#2696): asserts both classify entry points (ClassifyMachineToken, ClassifyMachineTokenByID) persist through SetMachineIdentityCredentialClassification and that its LocalStorage body is a Where+Updates with no Save and no Select("*"); UpdateMachineIdentityCredential is named as forbidden so re-adding the deleted full-row primitive turns this red. Runs without a Postgres DSN, so the fix is guarded in the default CI leg too

AzureKeyVaultConnector's client had no CheckRedirect override, so it followed a cross-host 301/302/303/307/308 redirect and trusted the redirected response as the secret value (credentials confirmed not to leak, but the response content was); found by response-fuzz harness construction, fixed by hardened_client.go's refuseRedirect wired into azurekv.go's client(); see docs/findings/2026-09-19-FINDING-connect-response-trust-gaps.md §2

AWSSecretsManagerConnector had no response-size bound; a gzip-bombed backend response (~2 MiB compressed) forced ~4 GiB peak heap via transparent decompression with err=nil; fixed by hardened_client.go's sizeCappedRoundTripper capping the decompressed body at connectMaxResponseBytes; see docs/findings/2026-09-19-FINDING-connect-response-trust-gaps.md §3

AzureKeyVaultConnector had no response-size bound; the same gzip-bomb shape forced ~3.6 GiB peak heap with err=nil; fixed the same way as the AWS sibling, wired into azurekv.go's client() via azsecrets.ClientOptions.Transport; see docs/findings/2026-09-19-FINDING-connect-response-trust-gaps.md §3

GCPSecretManagerConnector's real client() path inherited Google's SDK default of an effectively unbounded gRPC receive cap (grpc.MaxCallRecvMsgSize(math.MaxInt32)), unlike the AWS/Azure connectors' already-capped HTTP transport; found while ruling out a message-size cause for FuzzGCPSMConnectorResponse's CI OOM (the actual cause was a harness per-iteration leak, see docs/findings/2026-09-23-FINDING-gcpsm-fuzz-memory-and-recv-cap.md §1), fixed by appending an explicit grpc.MaxCallRecvMsgSize(1 MiB) dial default after Google's own; red/green-proved against the real grpc-go mechanism (bufconn + insecure creds), since option.WithGRPCConn bypasses dial-option processing entirely and ADC is unavailable in this environment; see §2 of the same finding doc
