Suspending, deactivating or deleting a user sweeps exactly two child tables (sessions via DeleteSessionsForUserExcept, personal_access_tokens via RevokeAllPersonalAccessTokensForUser) inside a transaction that row-locks the user first, but the INSERTS were not serialized against that sweep -- so a PAT minted in the window committed with revoked=false AFTER a sweep that was audited as complete. The PAT is inert while the account is blocked (ValidatePATToken re-checks account state), but ReactivateUser revokes nothing, so the routine suspend -> investigate -> reactivate sequence handed the credential back, possibly with no expiry. Fixed by inserting inside a transaction and re-reading the owner with lockLiveParent (FOR SHARE on Postgres) -- still is_active and still in a login-capable account_state -- rolling back if not. Sound because every sweep path row-locks the user BEFORE revoking, which lockLiveParent's write-then-check ordering requires. Red on real Postgres: one unrevoked PAT survived a suspend that reported success. Found by C-GUARD-3 guard 2

session half of credential-under-suspend-001 (#2701): a session committed after the suspend's DeleteSessionsForUserExcept swept the table is inert until reactivation and then live until its own expiry (RefreshSession can extend it to the absolute ceiling). RotateSession's freshly inserted row has the same exposure and gets the same re-check -- its CAS on rotated_at serializes it against another rotation, not against a credential sweep. Red on real Postgres: one live session survived a suspend that reported success

structural half of credential-under-suspend-001/002 (#2701): asserts all THREE credential-row inserts (CreatePersonalAccessToken, CreateSession, RotateSession) do their insert inside a transaction AND call requireLiveCredentialOwner, and that requireLiveCredentialOwner goes through lockLiveParent rather than a plain read (an unlocked re-read would not serialize against the sweep's LockUserForUpdate). The population of three is DERIVED and the derivation is written into the test: the sweep paths revoke exactly two tables, so the population is every LocalStorage method inserting into one of them, which a repo grep confirms is exactly those three (CreateSetupToken inserts a different table and is correctly out of scope). The account_state predicate reuses globalAdminLiveAccountStates -- the SAME slice, not a copy -- so TestGlobalAdminLiveAccountStates_MatchAccountLoginBlocked keeps it in step with core.AccountLoginBlocked and there is no second list to drift

SQLite half of credential-under-suspend-001 (#2701), on the production DSN (_txlock=immediate) so it runs in default CI: replica B's SuspendUser runs and commits in the window before replica A's PAT INSERT; a live unrevoked PAT must not survive. Red pre-fix (the autocommit INSERT held no lock, so the sweep fit in the window); green once the insert runs in a transaction. Siblings: TestCredentialUnderSuspend_CreateSession_vs_SuspendUser_CrossReplicaSQLite and TestCredentialUnderSuspend_CreatePAT_vs_DeleteUser_CrossReplicaSQLite (same file).

behavioural half of credential-under-suspend-001/002 (#2701), the sweep-committed-first ordering: once the owner is suspended, deprovisioned, is_active=false, in an unrecognized state, soft-deleted or missing, CreatePersonalAccessToken, CreateSession and RotateSession must each refuse AND leave no credential row; every login-capable state still mints (positive controls). Red with the owner re-check made a no-op, which the race tests cannot see on SQLite.

DeleteUser half of credential-under-suspend-001 (#2701) on Postgres: a PAT inserted while a concurrent DeleteUser sweeps must not survive unrevoked (delete -> restore -> reactivate would otherwise revive it). Covers the soft-delete case a weaker exists-and-blocked re-check would miss.

DeleteProjectIfEmpty counted the project's live secrets BEFORE taking the project row lock -- one call frame too late, since deleteProjectCascade already locked correctly before its own sweep but this function's own count ran before deleteProjectCascade was ever reached. This let CreateSecret's write-then-FOR-SHARE protocol (lockLiveParent) interleave with DeleteProjectIfEmpty: CreateSecret inserts and takes FOR SHARE uncontended (the count hadn't locked yet); DeleteProjectIfEmpty counts and sees 0 (the insert is still uncommitted, invisible under READ COMMITTED); DeleteProjectIfEmpty proceeds into the cascade, which blocks on the project row lock CreateSecret now holds; CreateSecret commits, reporting success; the cascade's lock then acquires and its FRESH secret sweep finds and soft-deletes the just-created secret as part of deleting the project. A non-force delete removed a project that, at the moment its caller was told "created", held a live secret. Fixed by extracting the project row-lock (lockProjectRowForCascade, Postgres-only) and calling it at the TOP of DeleteProjectIfEmpty's transaction, before the count, not only inside deleteProjectCascade -- forcing CreateSecret's own FOR SHARE re-check to wait for DeleteProjectIfEmpty's transaction regardless of which one started first. Proving test forces the exact interleaving via two independent Postgres connections synchronized with channels (not a blind scheduler-dependent race): RED (fix reverted) -- blockingSecretCount==0 and the project row is gone entirely, secret destroyed; GREEN (fix applied) -- blockingSecretCount==1, project survives, secret survives live and unreviewed.

ClassifyDynamicSecretConfig read a dynamic-secret config unlocked and persisted it through UpdateDynamicSecretConfig, a bare GORM Save of the whole row -- so `disabled=false` was written back over a concurrent SetDynamicSecretConfigEnabled(false), the incident kill switch that also revokes the config's live leases, and IssueLease could mint real database credentials again. The audit trail read "config_disabled" then only "classified"; nothing recorded the re-enable. The same column is what DeleteProject's #369 cascade sets, so the same write also re-enabled a config under a deleted project. Fixed by SetDynamicSecretConfigClassification, a conditional column-scoped UPDATE of classification alone gated on the value the caller read. Red on real Postgres with the full consequence demonstrated: disabled was false AND IssueLease successfully minted a new live credential after a disable that reported success. Found by C-GUARD-3 guard 1

sibling of dynamic-secret-kill-switch-revert-001 (#2698) on the lease table: RenewLease set ExpiresAt and persisted through UpdateDynamicSecretLease, a bare Save, writing the stale Status/RevokeError/RevokedAt back -- a concurrent successful RevokeLease became `active` again with a LATER expiry, so the row lied about a dead credential and kept holding a MaxActiveLeases slot until the sweep, and a revoke that had recorded `revoke_failed` was erased with its error. engine.Renew is a documented no-op on several backends (MySQL/Mongo/Redis), so nothing downstream would have noticed. Fixed by ExtendDynamicSecretLeaseExpiry: expires_at alone, WHERE lease_id=? AND status='active', with the renewal refused on no-match. The raw UPDATE normalises expires_at to UTC at the call site because it bypasses DynamicSecretLease.BeforeSave, which exists for ListExpiredActiveLeases' SQL range query (G81/INV-STORE-19). Red on real Postgres: status was active, revoked_at nil, and the lease still counted towards the active ceiling

structural half of dynamic-secret-kill-switch-revert-001/002 (#2698), and deliberately a DERIVED sweep rather than a per-function guard: it walks every non-test file under internal/core, internal/storage/store and server/ and asserts nothing calls the full-row UpdateDynamicSecretLease or UpdateDynamicSecretConfig, with exactly ONE named allowance (CreateDynamicSecretConfig's encrypted-DSN write, which is #2651's site and is moved by open PR #2675). It fails in BOTH directions -- a new caller appearing, and the allowance going stale -- so #2675 landing makes this test demand the allowance be dropped and both methods deleted. #2698 could not delete them itself without conflicting with #2675 in the same few lines. Companion TestDynamicSecretWrites_AreColumnScoped asserts the three new LocalStorage bodies are Where+Updates with no Save/Select("*") and that all three core entry points route through them

GCPEngine.Issue accepted a successful lease when generateAccessToken returned a nil error alongside an empty access_token -- the code only checked the error, never the token's content; fixed by rejecting when strings.TrimSpace(token) == ""; fuzz-confirmed (#2208)

UserGRPCService.projectCounts handled a RETURNED error from core.ProjectMembershipCounts but not a panic from the same call. userToProto calls it to build the RESPONSE for an already-created user, so a panic inside CountProjectMembershipsByUsers propagated past the committed User/UserRole/PasswordHistory/AuditEvent rows and RecoveryInterceptor turned it into Unavailable -- the caller saw an error for a request that had genuinely succeeded, with no returned ID to recover the user by. FuzzStorageFaultOperations found it on #2434 (oracle (a), differing tables [AuditEvent PasswordHistory User UserRole]). Fixed in #2408: projectCounts runs under besteffort.Run, so a panic yields absent (zero) counts rather than taking down the RPC; every userToProto caller (CreateUser, UpdateUser, GetUser, ListUsers) reaches it after its own primary write already committed, so the fix covers all four. Two independent non-vacuity checks, both run by FIX-2 against the pre-#2408 shape (besteffort.Run replaced by a direct call with only the returned error handled): the named proving test goes red, and the committed fuzz seed testdata/fuzz/FuzzStorageFaultOperations/5900200031 reproduces the issue's exact signature. That seed is index-addressed AND hash-named, so FIX-2 also registered it in seed_v2_test.go's seedIntent table -- without an entry it could silently re-point to another op/method on any storage-layer PR and keep passing under this claim's name, and its filename gives a reader no way to notice.

ChangePassword, ActivateMFA, and DisableMFA each spare the caller's own session from their post-change session purge by resolving keepSessionToken via storage.GetSession (`if s, serr := c.storage.GetSession(ctx, keepSessionToken); serr == nil { keepID = s.ID; keepHash = s.SessionToken }`). The `serr == nil` guard collapsed two different situations into one: keepSessionToken=="" ("no session to spare", keepID legitimately 0) and keepSessionToken!="" but GetSession failing (also keepID==0) -- both ended in the SAME full purge, including the caller's own session, with nothing distinguishing "the caller asked us not to spare a session" from "we could not tell which session to spare, so we killed them all". The widened purge is the correct fail-closed fallback (we cannot prove which session is the caller's, so revoking all of them is safer than guessing) and is NOT changed by this fix -- only its silence was. Worst case this masked: a storage hiccup on this one lookup during MFA activation could log the user out before the one-time recovery codes (returned in the response body, never stored in retrievable form) were ever displayed. Fixed by extracting resolution into resolveKeepSession (account.go), which now logs and writes EventKeepSessionLookupFailed when a supplied keepSessionToken fails to resolve, at all three call sites. The sibling finding -- deleteSessionsForUserAndEvict's own purge call failing outright (DeleteSessionsForUserExcept error), silently discarded by all 8 of its call sites -- is fixed at that function's own single choke point via the new EventSessionRevocationFailed, the returned-error analogue of the pre-existing EventSessionRevocationPanicked. Proving tests force each fault via a storage-wrapper stub: RED (audit-write lines removed) -- the lookup/purge failure still widens correctly but 0 audit rows are written; GREEN -- exactly 1 audit row per site, full purge unchanged. opScopedBestEffortTables (server/faultops) gained matching entries (GetSession on mfa/activate, mfa/disable, change-password; DeleteSessionsForUserExcept on mfa/disable, webauthn/register/finish), each gated on requireLogSubstring tied to the new log line -- a regression that silences the log would also silence the exemption, re-surfacing the oracle violation rather than being permanently waved through.

commitNewKEKFiles' rename-dek error cleanup unconditionally deleted kek.salt.pending on ANY rename error, without checking whether the rename had actually applied first (e.g. an NFS lost-reply/retransmit ambiguity) -- orphaning the DEK (every secret undecryptable) whenever it had. Fixed by dekRenameActuallySucceeded verifying actual on-disk content before cleanup; found by FuzzFaultInjectedOperations same PR as the fix (docs/findings/2026-09-19-FINDING-kek-rotation-rename-dek-cleanup-dataloss.md). landed_commit is a placeholder pending this branch's actual merge commit

Login/RefreshToken/VerifyMFA/BeginWebAuthnLogin/FinishWebAuthnLogin/FinishWebAuthnPasswordlessLogin all checked the per-IP login-attempt budget then ran the slow credential check (bcrypt/TOTP/WebAuthn assertion) and only recorded the attempt afterward, on failure only -- a concurrent burst from one IP all observed the same under-budget count at check time and blew through the budget before the counter caught up. Fixed by moving the record (renamed reserveLoginAttempt) to run before the slow step, right after the request is well-formed, at every affected call site; see docs/findings/2026-09-20-FINDING-login-lockout-mfa-recheck.md. Proving test REPOINTED by ORACLE-A-1 (#2816): this row named TestLogin_ConcurrentBurst_RateLimitBoundsCredentialChecks, whose statistical aggregate-429 assertion this PR removes as flaky-by-construction (overlapping distributions; 38 observed against a threshold of 40 under CI load). The ceiling is now asserted EXACTLY by the named test, which parks the whole per-IP budget inside its credential checks and shows the next request refused at the gate -- so the claim is proved by construction instead of by sampling. check-closures.sh would have stayed GREEN on the old name (the test still exists and passes), which is exactly why the row had to move: a closure whose proving test no longer asserts the claim is a green check that does not cover what its name implies.

G1 (FUZZ-GAPS) follow-up to login-rate-limit-reserve-first-001/PR #1981: that fix's own PR body flagged ConsumeSetup and BeginWebAuthnPasswordlessLogin as "explicitly out of scope" -- both shared checkLoginRateLimit's gate but never called reserveLoginAttempt at all, even pre-#1981, so unlike their six siblings neither ever contributed to the shared per-IP login-attempt budget and either could be hammered without limit, defeating the rate limiter as a brute-force/DoS throttle on those two endpoints specifically. Confirmed by FuzzLoginThrottleConcurrency (login_throttle_fuzz_test.go), a deterministic controlled-interleaving harness driving all 8 budget-sharing endpoints against a real storage-backed KeyorixCore and checking ground-truth login_attempts row counts (never wall-clock timing). Fixed by adding the same reserveLoginAttempt call, in the same position (after the minimal well-formedness check, before the slow step), to both call sites. Red-before/green-after: reverting both new reserveLoginAttempt calls made 9 of the harness's 11 corpus entries fail with "BUDGET NOT RESERVED"; restoring them passed all 11.

Logout (server/http/handlers/auth.go) blanket-mapped ANY error from core.Logout to 500 InternalError, including the ordinary case where the session was already deleted by a prior logout (a double-click, two tabs, or a client retry) -- confirmed live while building SESSION-N's N5 customer-journey test (real Keycloak OIDC login, then two logout calls with the same session cookie): the second call returned 500. Fixed by core.ErrSessionNotFound + errors.Is in the handler, returning 401 (an ordinary auth outcome) instead; TestLogout_InvalidToken_S8 tightened from accepting either 200 or 500 to asserting the now-deterministic 401. Logout has exactly one caller in this repo. See scripts/e2e/journeys/journey5_sso_login_test.go for the live end-to-end reproduction/regression.

LocalStorage.UpdateRotationPolicy was a bare GORM Save of a struct the caller read earlier. RotationPolicy IS soft-deletable, so Save's 0-rows fallback (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, deleted_at=NULL included) brought a concurrently deleted policy back ACTIVE -- resuming rotation and breach alerts although the delete had reported success. Fixed by UpdateRotationPolicyFields, a column-scoped UPDATE of the six operator-editable columns scoped to deleted_at IS NULL, with the caller failing closed on no-match. Red on real Postgres: a live policy row existed after a delete that reported success. Found by C-GUARD-3 guard 1

second consequence of the same #2700 primitive: the full-row Save also reverted rotation_state/last_rotation_error/last_state_at, which belong to UpdateRotationState (the rotation executor) -- so an ordinary policy edit erased a recorded rotation FAILURE, hiding it from the posture view that reads those columns. Closed by excluding those three columns from UpdateRotationPolicyFields entirely. Red on real Postgres: rotation_state was back to "idle" and last_rotation_error empty after an executor stamp that reported success

third #2700 site: core.UpdateSecretTemplate persisted through a bare Save, and SecretTemplate is HARD-deleted (no DeletedAt), so the 0-rows upsert fallback re-INSERTED a concurrently deleted template with its old id. Integrity only -- a template mints nothing by itself -- and the severity is low, stated as such rather than inflated. Fixed by UpdateSecretTemplateFields: a column-scoped UPDATE whose RowsAffected check IS the whole guarantee here, since there is no deleted_at to scope on. Red on real Postgres: the template row existed again after a delete that reported success

fourth #2700 site: markWebAuthnCredentialClonedDisabled (the disable-on-clone-signal mutation) persisted through a bare Save, and WebAuthnCredential is HARD-deleted, so a passkey the user removed inside the window was re-INSERTED. It comes back with Disabled=true so it FAILS CLOSED for authentication -- the damage is to the credential count and the webauthn_enabled bookkeeping derived from it, not access. Low severity, stated as such. Fixed by DisableWebAuthnCredential (disabled alone, RowsAffected-checked, deliberately unconditional on the current value since disabling is monotone); AdvanceWebAuthnCredentialCounter's sibling Save -- which #2700 classes SAFE because it holds SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in the same transaction -- moved to SetWebAuthnCredentialCounterState too, so the model has no full-row writer left at all. Red on real Postgres: the credential row existed again after a delete that reported success

structural half of low-severity-full-row-save-001..004 (#2700): asserts all four new LocalStorage bodies are Where+Updates with no Save and no Select("*"), and that the three core entry points route through them. All three full-row primitives (UpdateRotationPolicy, UpdateSecretTemplate, UpdateWebAuthnCredential) are DELETED in this PR -- unlike #2695/#2698, where one caller each belonged to another open PR and a no-remaining-caller sweep was needed instead -- so the guard names them as forbidden purely so re-adding one goes red rather than producing an unrelated build error. Runs without a Postgres DSN

TransitionMachineIdentity's post-commit, best-effort auth-cache eviction (internal/core/machine_identities.go) had no recover() around its MachineTokenHashes lookup, so a PANIC there (not just a returned error) unwound past an ALREADY-COMMITTED suspend/revoke, was caught by the outer HTTP Recovery middleware, and misreported a successful revoke as a 500 -- oracle (a). Found by FuzzStorageFaultOperations (server/faultops), fault=ListMachineIdentityCredentials#1/panic, crashing input ff58003231, now a permanent seed at server/faultops/testdata/fuzz/FuzzStorageFaultOperations/0134bc8cffdd0cfe. Confirmed the panic reproduces identically on the pre-existing fresh-per-call fuzz path too (not introduced by the in-flight world-reuse perf PR #2296 that found it faster). Fix: evictMachineIdentityCacheOrFlush recovers the panic and, on either a panic or a persistent lookup error after one retry, fails CLOSED by flushing every machine-token entry in the HTTP auth cache (InvalidateAllMachineTokenCache, server/middleware/auth.go) rather than silently leaving the revoked identity's credentials live in cache -- broader than a precise per-hash evict, but bounded to machine principals only (human sessions/PATs untouched) and self-healing (every machine principal simply re-validates against the DB on its next request, which correctly reflects the now-committed state). The proving test red/green-verified: fails on both halves (500 response, AND the revoked token still authenticating) with the recover() reverted, passes with it restored.

ValidateMachineToken (ADR-030) and ValidateOIDCToken (ADR-031) soft-failed a GetMachineRoles storage error into (machine, []string{}, nil) -- a successful-looking validation with an EMPTY role list, the exact fail-open #1944 removed from ValidatePATToken/ValidateSessionToken and which both machine paths were missed by. Not a privilege gain (zero roles only ever fails closed at core.Authorize) but a silent wrong answer the HTTP middleware then POSITIVELY CACHED as UserContext.Roles, and a machine-token cache HIT refreshes only the credential's restriction/revocation state, never its roles -- so one blip stripped a machine identity of every grant for the rest of validTokenTTL, reporting success throughout. Fixed by returning the existing ErrRoleResolutionUnavailable sentinel from both, plus mapping it to codes.Unavailable in validateGRPCMachineToken, which previously collapsed every ValidateMachineToken error into Unauthenticated + a peer-IP brute-force strike. Found by FIX-1's sibling sweep for #2548/#2567

SURFACE REMOVED (ADR-108 Phase 6 step 14c-2): proving test TestMarkTOTPStepUsedProxy_StepFarInFuture_Rejected deleted along with MarkTOTPStepUsedProxy (the /system POST mfa/totp-step-used relay route) this clock-skew bound protected. Confirmed (internal/core/mfa.go, ActivateMFA/VerifyMFACredentials) the local, non-proxy path never had this vulnerability shape to begin with: it calls c.storage.MarkTOTPStepUsed(ctx, userID, step) with step always internally computed by validateTOTPStep(secret, code) from a real cryptographic TOTP check, never accepted as a raw wire field the way the deleted proxy route did. See docs/findings/2026-09-23-FINDING-active-transition-admin-rank-totp-step-bound.md for the original finding.

mintSession (internal/core/auth.go) discarded a RETURNED error from its best-effort EnforceSessionLimit call but had no panic protection, so a panic there propagated past the already-committed Session row and out through the transport's panic-recovery wrapper as a 500 -- misreporting an already-successful login, and for the POST /auth/mfa/verify caller also an already-CONSUMED TOTP step, as a failure. FuzzStorageFaultOperations found it on #2392 (oracle (a), differing tables [LoginAttempt Session MFASecret]). Fixed in #2416: the call runs under besteffort.Run, which recovers a panic the same way the returned error was already absorbed. Every session-minting path funnels through mintSession (Login, setup-token consume x2, SSO complete, VerifyMFALogin), confirmed as the single EnforceSessionLimit call site in internal/core, so this closure covers the family and not just the MFA-verify instance. Two independent non-vacuity checks, both run by FIX-2 against the pre-#2416 shape (besteffort.Run replaced by a bare discarded call): the named proving test goes red, and the committed fuzz seed testdata/fuzz/FuzzStorageFaultOperations/mfa-verify-enforcesessionlimit-panic-2416 reproduces the issue's exact signature ("ORACLE (a) VIOLATION ... Differing tables: [LoginAttempt Session MFASecret]"). That seed is index-addressed, so FIX-2 also registered it in seed_v2_test.go's seedIntent table, without which it could silently re-point to a different op/method on any storage-layer PR and keep passing under this claim's name.

suspending a machine identity took effect only on the replica that ran it: CurrentMachineTokenRestriction returned a non-active owning identity as a bare fmt.Errorf which serveAuthCacheHit cannot distinguish from a storage blip, so the cache-hit path took the degrade-to-stale branch and the token kept authenticating for up to validTokenTTL (30s) on every other replica. Now core.ErrMachineIdentityNotActive, denied alongside the revoked/expired sentinels; the previously t.Skip-ped test is un-skipped in the same change

core half of mi-suspend-cachehit-001: every non-active machine identity state yields core.ErrMachineIdentityNotActive (errors.Is, not a message match), with both calibration directions - an active identity still succeeds, and a transient storage failure is NOT reported as the sentinel so a blip cannot start denying on the cache-hit path

MigrateUserToMachine created the machine identity in its own transaction and then suspended the source user in a second one, so any refusal or failure in the suspension left a new machine identity beside a still-ACTIVE human account with live sessions and PATs -- reported to the caller as a partial state for an operator to finish by hand. Reachable on ORDINARY input, not only under injected faults: the admin-rank ceiling (an actor who does not outrank the target) and guardLastAdminDeactivation (a last-admin target) were both evaluated AFTER the identity had committed. Fixed by hoisting both refusals and the input validation ahead of any write and committing the identity insert and the suspension in ONE WithTransaction inside the existing named lock, with cache eviction and all three audit events after commit; setAccountState was split into setAccountStateInTx (its transaction body, returning the hashes to evict) so the two writes can share a transaction without changing single-write behaviour. Three sibling tests cover the other angles: _UnderRankedActorCreatesNoIdentity and _LastAdminTargetCreatesNoIdentity (refused, zero identities, target unchanged) and _HappyPathCommitsBothAndAudits (so the three negative assertions cannot be satisfied by a function that never works). All four run against a real SQLite transaction, since a mock WithTransaction runs its closure inline and cannot demonstrate a rollback. Found by FIX-2 review on PR #2812; root-caused as an atomicity-guard detector gap (atomicityWriteVerbRe had no Suspend, so only one of the two writes was counted and the function never reached the 2-write threshold), fixed as a product change on coordinator decision rather than classified as an exemption.

IsLinkLocal (the narrower SSRF-target check used by the JWKS/OIDC egress guard and now internal/connect's hardened transport) did not decode NAT64 (64:ff9b::/96) or IPv4-compatible (::x) IPv6 encodings of an embedded link-local IPv4 -- only IsPrivateOrLinkLocal had that decode step (#1937/ssrf-nat64-ipv4compat-001); a NAT64-encoded cloud IMDS target would pass IsLinkLocal despite IsPrivateOrLinkLocal already rejecting it. Fixed by refactoring both predicates onto one shared matchesCIDRsWithEmbedded helper; found while implementing the Connect hardened-client link-local guard, which needed IsLinkLocal to have the same coverage IsPrivateOrLinkLocal already did

Moving NotificationChannel.URL (the webhook/Slack/Teams bearer credential) to encrypted-at-rest storage in url_enc introduced three ways to lose it, all because url_enc held either an encryption envelope or raw passthrough plaintext with nothing distinguishing them. notification_channels is the ONE encrypted auth-secret column whose write path cannot refuse when storage.encryption.enabled is off -- the feature predates encryption here -- so passthrough rows genuinely exist, unlike MFASecret (BeginMFAEnrollment fails closed on AuthEncryptionActive). Consequences, each confirmed red before this fix: (a) an upgrading install's email channel carries url='' in the legacy column, the backfill's `url != ''` predicate skipped it, and the fail-closed ListNotificationChannels then errored on the WHOLE list over that one URL-less row -- taking the channel UI, the CRUD API and RunRecoverAdminAlerting down together (observed: "failed to decrypt notification channel 1 URL: ... unexpected end of JSON input" with 1 of 2 rows migrated); (b) CreateNotificationChannel's insert and its encrypt-then-persist were two untransacted writes, so an encrypt failure left a durable row with an empty url_enc -- the same broken shape as (a), reachable with no upgrade at all (observed: 1 row persisted where 0 was required); (c) a row written with encryption OFF stored raw plaintext in url_enc, so enabling encryption later left it undecryptable AND hard-failed sweepNotificationChannels at DeserializeEncryptedData -- and SweepAllTables propagates, so DEK rotation broke for EVERY table, not just this one (observed: backfill re-ran over 0 rows, then "invalid character 'h' looking for beginning of value"). Fixed by making the at-rest format self-describing: ports.WrapNotificationChannelURL/UnwrapNotificationChannelURL prefix url_enc with a one-byte format tag (absent/plaintext/encrypted), an unrecognised tag is an error rather than a guess at which half is the URL, the read path maps absent to the empty URL and refuses an envelope when no encryptor is wired, CreateNotificationChannel's two writes share one WithTransaction (so the insertNotificationChannelRow indirection that hid its second write from TestAtomicityGuard_UnclassifiedMultiWriteFunction is gone, satisfying INV-CORE-35 for the real reason), the startup backfill covers every row including url='' and upgrades plaintext-tagged rows the first time encryption is enabled, and that backfill now FAILS STARTUP instead of logging-and-continuing -- a permanently failing run of its off-to-on job would otherwise leave webhook credentials in plaintext at rest on an install that explicitly configured encryption, still reading back fine so nothing else surfaces it (same reasoning as the SecretValueEncryptionActive refusal immediately above the call site).

Four post-commit best-effort storage writes were discarded with a bare `_ =`, which drops an error but not a panic: CreateUserWithAssignments' AddPasswordHistory (gRPC CreateUser reported Internal for a committed user + role grants), ChangePassword's Add/PrunePasswordHistory (a committed password change reported 500 and its PAT/session revocation never ran), CompleteSSO/CompleteSAML's RecordLogin (a live Session minted while the ACS reported 500) and cleanupOrphanedRole's revoke_failed lease write (a panic skipped the operator audit for a live orphaned role). All now run through besteffort.Run. Class guard: internal/besteffortguard no longer lets a blank-discarded write act as the last-write anchor, which is what hid every one of these from it (planted case MustFlagDiscardedWriteAfterWrite). Found by FuzzStorageFaultOperations (CI fuzz shard 2 on #2876, GRPC UserService.CreateUser AddPasswordHistory#1/panic); red on origin/main for all four fuzz tuples.

core.CreateSecret, core.CreateFolder, core.CreateEnvironment and LocalStorage.RestoreSecret each serialized only against a concurrent DeleteENVIRONMENT -- via the EnvironmentSecretGuardLockKey named lock plus an in-lock environment-existence check -- and never against a concurrent DeletePROJECT, whose cascade takes no such named lock: it row-locks the project and sweeps the project's secrets and environments directly. So the entirely legitimate order "cascade locks the project, sweeps the children that exist (the writer's is not inserted yet), commits; the writer then writes anyway" left a LIVE child under a deleted project. Reachable rather than merely untidy: GetSecret and AuthorizeSecret do not check project liveness, so a global-scope role or an ACL grant still reaches the value, the owner short-circuit still applies (IsProjectMember has no liveness join), new shares can still be made on it, and the purge only ever collects soft-deleted rows so the orphan outlives the project purge. Same end state as #2656, which fixed RestoreEnvironment alone. Fixed with that same lockLiveParent write-then-check, now reachable from internal/core through a new Storage.LockLiveProject -- the thin unchecked LocalStorage.CreateSecret contract is deliberately left alone, since a previous attempt to put a lock there was reverted for breaking the first-boot index test whose fixture has no projects table at all. This row is the structural default-ci half; the behavioural proof is four pg-gated two-replica tests, see project-child-liveness-create-restore-002. Mutation-proven in both directions: removing CreateEnvironment's re-check goes red on the re-check assertion, removing RestoreEnvironment's transaction wrapper goes red on the transaction assertion, and the guard is green on the fixed tree

The behavioural half of project-child-liveness-create-restore-001: two independent connection pools into one isolated schema, replica B running DeleteProject's full cascade between replica A's authorization and A's own child write. Four sites (#2702 CreateSecret, #2711 CreateFolder, #2710 CreateEnvironment, #2712 RestoreSecret); this row names the CreateSecret one, the other three are _CreateFolder_, _CreateEnvironment_ and _RestoreSecret_ in the same file. Each asserts the EFFECT -- the count of LIVE children under the deleted project -- not A's returned error, because A may legitimately fail OR be swept; what it may not do is leave a live child behind. The CreateSecret test additionally asserts no orphan version 1 survives, since the version is written in the same transaction. Each also asserts the interleaving actually happened (the one-shot hook fired) and that B's delete really committed, so a zero orphan count cannot be the vacuous consequence of the delete having failed. Red-proven by neutering the project re-check to answer "live" unconditionally -- the pre-fix behaviour, nothing else changed: all four go red with exactly one orphan child each, plus the orphan version. NOT covered, and stated in the file header rather than left to be assumed: the opposite interleaving where A's FOR SHARE lands first and the cascade blocks on it -- lockLiveParent's doc argues that order is safe, and the beforeA hook can only produce the order that caused the bug

deleteProjectCascade's #2656 project FOR UPDATE was written with GORM's default scope, which appends deleted_at IS NULL, so on an ALREADY-deleted project it matched zero rows and locked NOTHING -- exactly the case where a concurrent RestoreProject has to be excluded. RestoreProject took no project-row lock either; the row was locked only by its own final UPDATE, after both child UPDATEs had run. Every other cascade statement is deleted_at IS NULL-scoped too, so under READ COMMITTED the sweeps skipped (snapshots saw deleted children), the restore committed, and the cascade's final UPDATE projects took a fresh statement snapshot, saw the project live and deleted it -- leaving every restored environment and secret LIVE under a deleted project, which no serial order produces. Consequences are #2702/#2710/#2712's: reachable via global-scope roles, ACLs and the owner short-circuit, never purged, outlives the project purge. Fixed by locking the project row by id UNSCOPED on both sides, before any child write, with the cascade reading its liveness verdict off the row it just locked instead of folding deleted_at IS NULL into the locking query -- that folding is what made the lock vacuous. The guard checks Unscoped() specifically, because a guard asserting only "takes clause.Locking" would have been GREEN for the bug's entire lifetime; it also pins the premise that locking in the shared cascade covers both DeleteProject and DeleteProjectIfEmpty (#528). Red-proven by reverting Unscoped() while keeping the lock -- the original defect verbatim -- which the guard reports by name. #2724's second path (RestoreProject does not take EnvironmentSecretGuardLockKey) is recorded in the INVARIANTS fragment and left open: its precondition is a live environment under a deleted project, which is the #2702/#2710 state that #2881 closes

The behavioural half of project-row-lock-unscoped-001: replica A holds the project row with the same unscoped FOR UPDATE the fix added, and replica B's DeleteProject cascade must not complete until it is released. Asserts the MECHANISM (mutual exclusion on the project row) rather than the forbidden end state, and that choice is deliberate and load-bearing. An end-state test was written -- 14 iterations racing RestoreProject against DeleteProject, asserting "never (project deleted AND live children)" -- and DELETED after the red proof showed it never reproduced the orphan state even with the fix reverted: it failed only on its own non-vacuity floor, i.e. it reported that the scenario had not occurred. Unsynchronized goroutines do not hit a window this narrow. A deterministic version is impossible by construction rather than merely hard: the interleaving needs the restore to COMMIT between the cascade's child sweeps and its final project UPDATE, which a one-shot GORM-callback hook can arrange only for the BROKEN code -- after the fix the cascade holds the project row from its first statement, so a hooked restore blocks inside the cascade's own callback and the test hangs instead of passing. Shipping the end-state test would have read as coverage of exactly the thing it never exercised. Red-proven: with the pre-fix shape restored on both sides (scoped cascade lock, unlocked restore read) this test fails with "DeleteProject's cascade completed while another replica held the project row", err=project not found. Its held transaction is released through t.Cleanup, not only on the happy path, after an equivalent leak in the break-glass lock-wait test hung a parallel test for a full 600s timeout instead of failing

recover-admin (server/admin/recover_admin_logic.go), the one documented emergency-recovery mechanism for a locked-out admin, cleared the target account's password hash to "" with nothing to replace it. bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword (internal/core/auth.go's VerifyPasswordCredentials) fails unconditionally against an empty hash for every password, so the recovered account could never actually log back in through any documented path -- the one official recovery mechanism was itself a permanent self-DoS on admin access. Found live (design-b2-recover-admin.md's own §3 already claimed "the very first thing the recovered admin can do is log in, set a password" -- never actually true). Fixed by setting a server-generated one-time password (core.GenerateInitialCredential, the same generator CreateUserWithOneTimePassword already uses for new-user onboarding, ADR-028 Part E, hashed at core.PasswordHashCost) instead of an empty hash, printed once for the operator to relay, while keeping password_reset_required so every OTHER endpoint stays refused until a real password is chosen. Red-before/green-after proving test drives the full documented sequence through the real internal/core login/change-password code (not a re-implementation of it): recover-admin -> log in with the printed OTP -> forced password change -> log in with the new password -> confirm the superseded OTP no longer works.

Under the default security.require_mfa, a restricted account with no second factor (recover-admin's recovered admin, a one-time-password user, an admin-forced reset, pending first login) could never leave the restricted state: EnforceAccountRestriction refused /auth/mfa/enroll with PasswordChangeRequired and EnforceMFAEnrollment refused /auth/change-password with MFAEnrollmentRequired, so the documented lost-admin runbook ended in a permanent lockout whose only exits were insecure (require_mfa:false) or a backup restore. Replaced by one gate, server/middleware.EnforceAccountSetup, over core.PendingAccountSetupSteps: the union of the pending steps' routes (exact method + full path) plus GET profile, 403 with pending_steps on everything else. A login owing both steps gets a SetupOnly session capped at core.SetupSessionTTL (15 min, carried through refresh), revoked by core.EndSetupSessionIfComplete when the last step completes, so the next login is a normal two-step MFA login; an ordinary session owing both steps, or a SetupOnly session owing none, is refused 401. Found along the way and fixed in the same change: the ChangePassword handler tombstoned the caller's KEPT session in the auth cache (401 for invalidTokenTTL right after a password change, the #2978 bug class); now a delete-only clear. Proving tests: the route-registry guard (walks every /api/v1 route of the real router, red on main because the 403 carried no pending steps and mfa/enroll was refused) and TestAccountSetup_EitherOrder_EndsInMFALogin (every restricted population x both orders, red on main at the enrolment/password step); e2e scripts/e2e/journeys/journey20_recover_admin_mfa_test.go on the shipped config.

#3041 review: after a session token validated, the HTTP auth middleware re-read the session row for its setup-only flag (and, in separate reads, its impersonator and expiry) and on a failed read served the request with SetupOnly=false, no impersonator and no expiry clamp, and cached that identity. A setup-only session whose revocation had not landed (or failed) then had full API access the moment the store faltered and kept it from the cache after the store recovered. Now one read, core.ResolveSessionAuthFacts, supplies every per-session fact; a failed read refuses the request with 503 (nothing cached, no brute-force strike) and is logged and audited as auth.session_facts_unavailable. EndSetupSessionIfComplete no longer discards a failed revocation: its completion event says the sessions could not be revoked. Red before: 200 with the store faulted, 200 again from the cache after it recovered, no audit row.

#3041 review: the gRPC auth interceptor never checked models.Session.SetupOnly, so a setup-only session (#3024) that had finished both setup steps but whose revocation had not landed passed every gRPC gate with full access (HTTP refused it with ReauthenticationRequired). The interceptor now applies the HTTP setup gate's rules through enforceGRPCAccountSetup: gRPC has no setup-step RPC, so a setup-only session is refused every RPC (PermissionDenied while steps are owed, Unauthenticated once nothing is owed), and an ordinary session owing both steps is sent to sign in again; its per-session facts come from core.ResolveSessionAuthFacts and a failed read answers Unavailable, audited. The guard walks every RPC the real server registers (GetServiceInfo) with a setup-only session and pins the allowed set (expectedSetupGRPCMethods, empty). Red before: e.g. AuditService/GetAuditLogs answered OK to a setup session that owed nothing.

core.RestoreGroup read GetGroupRoles and ran requireGlobalAdminToReinstateAdminRoles, then called storage.RestoreGroup separately and unlocked: a role grant to the still-soft-deleted group landing in that window is invisible to the ceiling check, so a non-global-admin actor's restore passes against a stale (pre-grant) role set and resurrects a group already carrying an admin-conferring role. Reachable because the storage-level write (assignGroupRole, local_rbac.go) never checks the target group's existence or soft-delete state, so a JIT/time-bound grant lands on a soft-deleted group happily. Fixed in #2469 by running the read, the check and the restore write all under sodGrantLockKey("group", id) -- the same key AssignRoleToGroup/AssignGroupRoleWithExpiry already take. Proving test is the pg-gated CROSS-REPLICA one named here, not the SQLite deterministic sibling (TestConcurrency_RestoreGroup_AdminGrantRace_TOCTOU_Deterministic): on SQLite WithNamedLock is an in-process mutex in ONE LocalStorage, so no single-process harness can distinguish a working lock from a deleted Postgres branch -- verified by disabling that branch, which leaves the SQLite test green and turns this one red. FIX-2 also repaired a real vacuity in that SQLite sibling, which passed 3/3 with the WithNamedLock wrapper deleted outright because it paused inside the restore's own write transaction and SQLite's single-writer serialization blocked the racer by itself; its pause moved to WithTransaction entry and it now goes red 3/3 under the same mutation.

F3c: RBACHandler.CreateRole's own permission-assignment loop had the same discard-and-log shape as F3a's replaceRolePermissions -- swallowed every AssignPermissionToRole error, always replying 201 regardless. Found live by coverage-batch-5's fuzz burst wiring REST POST /api/v1/roles/ into the operation catalog: a fault on AssignPermissionToRole's own actor-authority resolution produced a successful 201 with "permissions":null -- an oracle (c) fail-closed-authz violation, not just oracle (a). Fixed by making core.CreateRole run the role-row create and every AssignPermissionToRole call inside one storage.WithTransaction, propagating any failure as an error and auditing only after commit; both REST and gRPC now call this single function. Proving test is the fuzz harness itself -- corpus entry c600067cf4d3bb8e is the permanent regression, no KNOWN-OPEN tolerance needed; see docs/findings/2026-09-21-FINDING-role-update-permission-replace-swallows-storage-errors.md

F3d: both core.UpdateRole's and core.CreateRole's final GetRolePermissions call (building the response's permission list) ran AFTER their own storage.WithTransaction committed and after audit logging -- a fault there reported an ERROR to the caller while the role update/create and its audit trail had already committed (oracle (a): AuditEvent table differs). Found live by an unattended fuzz burst smoke-testing coverage batch 6's two new /system ops (it found this instead, one call further down the already-fixed UpdateRole path); CreateRole had the structurally identical gap, fixed proactively before a second live finding. Fixed by moving each function's final GetRolePermissions read to be the LAST statement inside its own storage.WithTransaction closure, so a fault there rolls the whole operation back instead of reporting error-after-commit. Proving test is the fuzz harness itself -- corpus entry 637f47f4387c3138 is the permanent regression; see docs/findings/2026-09-21-FINDING-role-update-permission-replace-swallows-storage-errors.md. Regression-corpus fidelity note (2026-09-27): ADR-108 Phase 6 step 14c's opCatalog shrink (removing 7 /system-proxy-only ops) silently retargeted this corpus file's decoded operation from "REST POST /api/v1/rotation-policies/" to an unrelated op -- repaired by re-encoding the file's byte[0] to the same op's new index, verified to decode back to the original op/method/NthCall/kind tuple; guarded going forward by TestOpcatalogCorpusFilesTargetPinnedOps (server/faultops/opcatalog_corpus_pin_test.go).

F3a: RBACHandler.replaceRolePermissions (server/http/handlers/rbac.go) swallowed every storage error from RemovePermissionFromRole/AssignPermissionToRole and UpdateRole always replied 200 regardless; found by FuzzStorageFaultOperations's own seed corpus (predicted from code review, then confirmed live). Fixed by making core.UpdateRole run the role-row update and the permission-set replacement inside one storage.WithTransaction, propagating any failure as an error; both REST and gRPC now call this single function. Proving test is the fuzz harness itself, not a dedicated point test -- its seed corpus is the permanent regression, no KNOWN-OPEN tolerance remains; see docs/findings/2026-09-21-FINDING-role-update-permission-replace-swallows-storage-errors.md

F3b: same call site as -001, faulted with a panic instead of a returned error -- correctly turned into a 500 by the real Recovery middleware, but core.UpdateRole's own audit-log write (previously committed synchronously BEFORE permission replacement even ran) survived the panic that failed everything after it, leaving an AuditEvent asserting success behind a 500 response; found by an unattended 10-minute fuzz burst (not a hand-written seed), minimized input saved at server/faultops/testdata/fuzz/FuzzStorageFaultOperations/bdbfad52d4cc7bae; fixed by the same transaction restructuring as -001 (audit only written after commit); see docs/findings/2026-09-21-FINDING-role-update-permission-replace-swallows-storage-errors.md

ParseResponse accepted a validly-signed response with bytes appended after its root element (XML epilogue) unrejected by either our own XML-DSig path or crewjam/saml's internal xrv.Validate (token-round-trip check, not document-structure check); found by the new FuzzParseResponse harness (#1889) on day one, fixed same PR via validatePostedResponseHasNoEpilogue

DeprovisionSCIMUser (the IdP offboarding path) swept SESSIONS only -- it never called RevokeAllPersonalAccessTokensForUser, unlike every other deprovisioning path (setAccountState's blocked-state branch, DeleteUser, RevokeUserCredentialsForDeactivation), all of which revoke both. A surviving PAT is inert while the account is deprovisioned (ValidatePATToken re-checks is_active and the account state), but ReactivateUser and RestoreUser deliberately revoke nothing on the assumption the deprovision already did -- so an IdP offboard followed by a restore handed every PAT back, possibly with no expiry, after an audit trail recording a completed deprovision. Fixed by revoking in the SAME transaction (keeping SCIM DELETE all-or-nothing) and folding the hashes into the existing post-commit auth-cache eviction. Red on PRISTINE origin/main with only the test added: the PAT AUTHENTICATED after a restore. Found by RACE-FIX-2 while fixing #2701, which flagged it as "related, not a race"

the pre-existing test for #2855's property, strengthened. It was already NAMED RevokesSessionAndPAT and its doc comment already claimed "unable to authenticate via ANY credential", but it only asserted that ValidatePATToken returns an ERROR -- which it does regardless, because a deprovisioned account is login-blocked and soft-deleted. So it proved INERTNESS while its name promised REVOCATION, and passed identically with the revoke call absent. That is exactly how the gap survived review. It now also asserts the ROW state (no unrevoked PAT remains), which is the assertion that could have caught it. Red on pristine origin/main. Recorded as its own claim because "a green test named for the property" is the failure mode worth having in the ledger, not just the missing call

DeleteSecret handler (server/http/handlers/secrets_crud.go) unconditionally routed through the per-user owner/sharing permission check (userID != 0 required), so any machine-identity-authenticated caller got a misleading 500 on every delete regardless of the route's own scoped-permission gate; sibling handlers (GetSecret/GetSecretByName/GetSecretValueByRef) already had the correct isMachine bypass, DeleteSecret was the one call site missing it; found by the #1808 tranche-2 differential conformance harness (server/http/remote_storage_*_test.go, deleted ADR-108 Phase 6 step 14a) -- re-pointed at handlers_test.go's own direct DeleteSecret coverage rather than retired, since the fixed code path (secrets_crud.go, server/http/handlers, NOT the deleted proxy) is still live and still needs a proving test

DeleteSecret/RestoreSecret's shared emitDependencyLifecycleEvents helper (internal/core/secret_dependencies.go) correctly treated a returned error from its own best-effort ListSecretDependenciesForProject call as non-fatal (its own doc comment says so), but had no protection against a PANIC from that same call -- a panic propagated straight through DeleteSecret/RestoreSecret (which had already committed the delete/restore several lines earlier) and out to the real Recovery middleware, producing an honest-looking 500 that actually masked an already-successful delete/restore (oracle (a): SecretNode state changed despite a reported error). Found live by an unattended final-checks fuzz burst. Fixed by recovering from a panic in emitDependencyLifecycleEvents the same way it already handled a returned error -- log and return, never surface to the caller. Proving test is the fuzz harness itself -- corpus entry 059212c4cda84764 is the permanent regression; see docs/findings/2026-09-22-FINDING-secret-delete-restore-dependency-emission-panic-masks-success.md

UpdateSecret's full-struct Save() re-sent the caller's stale read_count, so an unrelated metadata edit refunded reads against a MaxReads burn-after-N-reads cap (#133) without any authority over the cap. Fixed by Omit(secretNodeSQLOwnedColumns...) at both full-struct writers; 3/3 red on unmodified main
sibling of secret-max-reads-refund-001: TransitionSecretStatus's Select("*").Updates(secret) had the identical defect for the identical reason — a status transition refunded a read against the cap

structural half of secret-max-reads-refund-001/-002: type-checks package store (go/types) and fails any Save/Updates/UpdateColumns whose argument's static type is a SecretNode and whose chain does not Omit(secretNodeSQLOwnedColumns...). States the call shapes it recognises and the three it deliberately does not; asserts it inspected >= 2 writers so it cannot pass vacuously

AccountLoginBlocked and AccountRestricted are not the same predicate (pending_first_login/password_reset_required are restricted but not login-blocked) -- a session cache hit's pre-existing account-usability check only re-verified the login-blocked boolean, never refreshed the cached AccountState/Restricted, so a transition into a restricted-but-not-blocked state (e.g. an admin's RequirePasswordReset) stayed invisible to EnforceAccountRestriction on a cache hit; fixed by core.AccountUsabilityAndState / cloneUserContextWithAccountState; see docs/findings/2026-09-20-FINDING-session-revoke-cache-race.md

serveAuthCacheHit's session branch only re-checked the owning account's state, never whether the session row itself still existed -- RevokeUserSessions and 6 sibling call sites (ChangePassword, ActivateMFA/DisableMFA, WebAuthn enrollment/removal, both setup-token-consume paths, the /system proxy's DeleteSessionsForUserExcept) could leave a deleted session authenticating via a stale positive cache entry; fixed by core.SessionLiveForToken wired into serveAuthCacheHit; found by FuzzConcurrentOpsLinearizable, landed same PR; see docs/findings/2026-09-20-FINDING-session-revoke-cache-race.md

the same session-liveness chokepoint closes the ADR-039-documented cross-replica cache-staleness bound (a revoke on one replica leaving the session live on another for up to validTokenTTL) down to the next request, since SessionLiveForToken re-reads from the same shared DB every replica already writes to; two cores sharing one DB, only one with the cache invalidator wired, prove a replica that never heard about a sibling's revoke still denies on its next cache hit; see docs/findings/2026-09-20-FINDING-session-revoke-cache-race.md

resolveSSOUser's first-federation path read the user with GetUserByEmail (unlocked, no transaction), set ExternalID, and persisted it through the full-row LocalStorage.UpdateUser (a GORM Save) -- against an account an admin deleted after that read, Save's UPDATE matched 0 rows and its upsert fallback wrote deleted_at=NULL, is_active=true, account_state=active, resurrecting the account; CompleteSSO's login gate then evaluated the STALE in-memory struct (still active) and minted a session for it. The user controls the timing: they fire the first SSO login, and can fire several in parallel. Same window also reverted a concurrent suspension, password change, MFA enable or lockout. Fixed in two parts, both required: ClaimUserExternalIDIfUnset writes external_id alone, conditional on it still being unset AND the row still being live; and resolveSSOUser then RE-READS through GetUser so the login gate acts on the committed row, failing closed (and not falling through to auto-provision) when the account is gone. Red on real Postgres before the fix on both halves: the row came back AND the returned user was login-capable. Sibling of #2677. Found by C-GUARD-3 guard 1

structural half of sso-first-federation-resurrect-001 (#2699): asserts resolveSSOUser persists through ClaimUserExternalIDIfUnset (a Where+Updates LocalStorage body with no Save and no Select("*")), never reaches UpdateUser or a bare Save, AND re-reads via storage.GetUser. The re-read is asserted separately on purpose -- it is the half that stops a session being minted for a deleted account, and a guard on the write shape alone would certify half a fix. Runs without a Postgres DSN

IsPrivateOrLinkLocal (shared SSRF blocklist for dynamic-secrets admin-DSN dials, Azure KMS dials, validateAdminDSNHost) accepted NAT64 (64:ff9b::/96) and IPv4-compatible (::x) IPv6 encodings of private/loopback/IMDS IPv4 (e.g. 64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe = IMDS 169.254.169.254); To4 folds only IPv4-mapped. Fixed by decoding the embedded IPv4 and checking it (not a wholesale-prefix block, so public NAT64 egress is preserved); found by adversarial probe building the DSN SSRF fuzzer, locked by FuzzIPv4EmbeddingSSRFParity (#1937)

LocalStorage.UpdateGroup was a bare GORM Save of a struct read earlier and unlocked; Save's 0-rows fallback upserts with deleted_at=NULL, and DeleteGroup deliberately RETAINS a deleted group's GroupRole/UserGroup rows so RestoreGroup can work -- so a rename landing after a delete or SCIM deprovision brought the group back with every role grant and membership live, with no restore audit event and without going through RestoreGroup. An IdP DELETE followed closely by a PUT/PATCH is enough: core.UpdateGroup, ReplaceSCIMGroup and PatchSCIMGroup all renamed through this primitive, outside the withGroupProjectAdminGuardLocks that deleteGroupGuarded holds. Fixed by replacing it with UpdateGroupFields, a conditional column-scoped UPDATE of only the non-nil fields, scoped to deleted_at IS NULL, with the caller failing closed on no-match and re-reading the committed row. Red on real Postgres: the group row was live again and carried its still-present grants. Found by C-GUARD-3 guard 1

LocalStorage.UpdateProject was a bare GORM Save, so a plain project RENAME whose read predated an admin enabling ADR-037's per-project require_mfa wrote `false` back over it -- silently disabling the per-project MFA requirement. The caller needs no roles.assign (only the rename route's own permission), and no audit event is written, because core.UpdateProject only audits when ITS OWN requireMFA argument differs from the value it read -- which it does not when the argument is nil. Fixed by UpdateProjectFields, a conditional column-scoped UPDATE that keeps requireMFA a POINTER all the way to the SET list, so "I am not changing this flag" never reaches the UPDATE. LocalStorage.UpdateSecret was a bare GORM Save of a struct the caller read earlier and unlocked, and it was the SHARED primitive for eight operations, so every one inherited its defects. Resurrection half: Save's 0-rows fallback upserts with deleted_at=NULL, so ANY of the eight landing after a concurrent DeleteSecret brought the secret back -- and DeleteSecret also revokes the secret's shares and ACLs, so it returned WITHOUT them, with no secret.restored audit event, without going through RestoreSecret, invisible to the restore UI and never reclaimed by the purge (which only takes deleted rows). Fixed by replacing the primitive with UpdateSecretFields, a per-field-pointer conditional UPDATE scoped to deleted_at IS NULL, with every caller naming only the columns it owns. Red on PRISTINE origin/main with only the test file added: the secret row was live again after a delete that reported success. Found by C-GUARD-3 guard 1

Review finding against #2700's own fix in the same branch, never on main. #2700 correctly replaced markWebAuthnCredentialClonedDisabled's full-row GORM Save (whose 0-rows upsert fallback re-INSERTED a hard-deleted passkey) with a column-scoped conditional UPDATE, and in doing so added early returns on !matched and on err != nil that sat BEFORE the EventWebAuthnCloneDetected audit write. The Save it replaced always reached that write, so a signature-counter regression stopped leaving any audit trail at all whenever the credential was deleted -- or the database briefly failed -- in the window between the assertion check and the disable. rejectIfCloned discards this function's error, so the failure mode was pure silence with a successful-looking login refusal. The regression was also covered by a comment claiming rejectIfCloned already audits the clone signal for the credential-missing case; it does not -- that else branch fires only on a failed LOOKUP, never on a lookup that succeeded and an UPDATE that then matched nothing. Fixed by writing the clone-detected audit UNCONDITIONALLY before any branch can return, with what happened to the row in the detail (disabled / already deleted / could NOT be disabled, treat as unmitigated). Deliberately NOT split into a second webauthn.error event: the clone verdict was already reached before this function was called, so there is exactly one incident, and a second event would let incident counts double -- the mfa.error/mfa.failed split exists for the opposite case where no verdict was reached. Both subtests assert the EFFECT (an audit row exists, with a detail that does not claim a mitigation that did not happen) because no return value in the chain distinguishes audited from silently skipped. The deleted-credential subtest reproduces the real interleaving against a real database -- a store wrapper returns the genuine row from the lookup and hard-deletes it, so the following UPDATE matches zero rows -- and drives the full rejectIfCloned path, so the discarded error is inside the subject. Red-proven by reinstating #2700's early returns: both subtests go red with ZERO audit events

Both WebAuthn login paths (FinishWebAuthnLogin, FinishWebAuthnPasswordlessLogin) minted the session and an unconditional ambient MFAStepUpGrant (Purpose = MFAStepUpPurposeRestrictedSecretRead) and only THEN handed back to the HTTP handler, which resolved the response identity (GetUserIdentity -> GetUserRoles + GetUserPermissions) for its body. A failure in THAT read was reported to the caller as a failed login (HTTP 500) while both writes stayed: completeLogin revoked the session but nothing revoked the grant, so a step-up grant outlived a login the caller was told had failed -- satisfying the restricted-secret MFA gate for the rest of the step-up window on some later session the user never proved a second factor for. Found by FuzzStorageFaultOperations (op="REST POST /auth/webauthn/login/finish", fault=(GetUserRoles, NthCall=1, kind=error)), confirmed by byte-for-byte replay against unmodified origin/main, and tolerated as an oracle (a) known-open entry until this fix (that tolerance row is removed by the same change). Fixed by ORDERING, not a second compensation: core.resolveLoginIdentityBeforeMint performs the read before the session/grant/step-up-token writes and returns the identity, which the handler uses via completeLoginWithIdentity instead of re-reading -- so no fallible-and-reported step runs after the writes and there is no partial state to undo. New sentinel core.ErrLoginIdentityUnavailable keeps the caller-visible shape identical (same 500, same message) and is deliberately NOT ErrWebAuthnLoginNotEvaluated, so the per-IP login-attempt reservation stays counted exactly as before (the assertion WAS evaluated and passed). Red/green: planting the original shape (read moved back after the grant mint) fires all three arms of the proving test (grant, session, step-up token); planting the intermediate shape (read after mintSession only) fires the session arm; both the passwordless sibling test and the oracle (a) harness with the tolerance removed go red too. Calibration companions stop the fix being made in the wrong direction -- TestFinishWebAuthnLogin_ReturnsAPopulatedIdentityForARoleHolder (the returned identity must be the real one, not UserIdentity{}, which would silently strip every user's roles from the login response) and server/faultops TestWebAuthnLogin_SuccessfulLoginStillMintsItsStepUpGrant (a successful login must still mint the grant; deleting the mint is not the fix). Passwordless path covered by the sibling TestFinishWebAuthnPasswordlessLogin_IdentityReadFailureLeavesNoSessionOrGrant -- that op is not in server/faultops' opCatalog, so its faultops subtest skips with a message naming this core test. SIBLING SWEEP: the same window existed on the TOTP path (VerifyMFALogin, /auth/mfa/verify), which mints no grant but DOES write a user-scoped MFAStepupToken that HasActiveMFAStepup reads per-USER rather than per-session -- same gate, same cross-session reach. Fixed identically and guarded by TestVerifyMFALogin_IdentityReadFailureLeavesNoSessionOrStepUpToken (red on both the token and session arms when the read is moved back after the writes). The remaining two completeLogin callers (Login, ConsumeSetup) write only the session, which completeLogin's existing revoke already covered, so they are unchanged -- established by enumerating what each caller writes after minting, not by assuming the first site found was the only one.
